title: Was Col. Kurtz the most rational character in Apocalypse Now?

commenti.body:
You sound like Captain Willard!

I'm not sure I'd call Kurtz "rational". I would still argue that he's an outright villain, and I don't think there's anything rational about genocide. But the thing that makes him stand out is that he's one of the only people in the movie who isn't bullshitting. He is a monster and he is taking part in monstrous act - the Vietnam War. He's realised who and what he is where everyone around him, and especially the US government, is acting virtuous, or appreciating the seriousness of what is happening around them.

By the end of the film, after everything he's seen, Willard is right there with him. The real turning point is when Lance guns down an innocent family, and Chief expects them to treat the survivor's wounds afterwards. The hypocrisy of the rest of the boat is clear as day.

I think it's important to understand the context with which the film came out. The Vietnam War was a disaster and it was pretty clear that America wasn't doing anything noble or heroic by taking part in it. The national mask had slipped and I think Kurtz kind of embodies the true face of America
[removed]

Haha maybe my world view is too nihilistic. Honest is probably a better term than rational for Kurtz. However, I'm not sure I see Kurtz as more of a villain than other Americans in high positions like Kilgore and the general, although he's without a doubt a lot farther down the path of lunacy than them. The film does nothing to support the fact that the American Army is more virtuous than him, only that he is rogue and needs to be terminated. The general starts Willard's journey by saying his methods are "unconventional" and then we get a 40 some minute sequence of American choppers mowing down villagers.
[removed]
Oh, I wouldn't say that Kurtz is *more* of a villain than characters like Kilgore. They're both mass murderers. The difference is that Kilgore hasn't recognised it in himself where Kurtz has
Wasn't Mr. Clean the one who guns down the family on the boat?
You're right, my bad. Lance is the one who grabs the dog

He may be the most honest character apart from what Willard eventually becomes at the end of the journey, but he clearly "enjoyed" what he was doing at one point and now recognizes that he deserves to die for it.  I need to re-read Heart of Darkness to see if Kurtz character in the book is "honest" as the movie version. I did a compare/contrast essay on the book/movie as an undergrad, but it was pretty surface level English 101 stuff.
[removed]

What do you mean by saying that Kurtz embodies the true face of American? In the movie there is evidence of him being an iconoclast and rejecting American ideals, but do you mean that after rejecting these ideals he's the more honest representation of America?
Definitely need to pick up the book somewhere. Do you know if it's widely available?
Any bookstore or library will have it.
I agree.  If you are driving a car and someone pops out of a side street, even though you have the right of way you are supposed to stop if you can.  Kurtz did not stop.

What I mean is that America presents itself righteous, good, and noble. At the very least that is how it wants its citizens to feel about the country. And I think for a lot of people in America that is how they felt, but the Vietnam War presented a stark realisation that it this was not the case.

The Penguin 'Vintage' edition comes doubled up with another novella by Conrad called 'Youth' which is also worth reading as a companion piece. The foreword also provides some historical context to Heart of Darkness that may change your view about Kurtz being rational.

I think there is something rational to Kurtz, but it isn’t what I would think of as the “most” rational approach to his situation. Like, if we’re buying into the cruelty necessary for that kind of war, then yes, doing so in a way that is coldly efficient, that deemphasizes the value of human life both in the enemy and in your own soldiers, that is the way that most assuredly leads to victory.

Of course, most rational people, when faced with this possibility, instead reject the context. “If this is what it takes to fight this kind of war, then this isn’t the kind of war I want to be fighting in the first place.”

Good point of rejecting the context. This is probably the sentiment that lead to mass demonstration in the US. However Kurtz wasn't afraid to humanize soldiers as he had come to terms with death and suffering as an instrument confined in the rules of warfare.

I’ve also read Heart of Darkness. But in my experience, the literary character who comes closest to Marlon Brando’s portrayal in the film is Judge Holden, in Cormac McCarthy’s Blood Meridian. They are both very rational, literate and thoughtful, and they have made peace with the evil of their professions. But the Judge probably takes his reasoning even further, or rather he is what Kurtz would be like if his last scrap of fellow feeling were to disappear.

> Willard: They told me that you had gone totally insane, and that your methods were unsound.
> Kurtz: Are my methods unsound?
> Willard: I don't see any method at all, sir.

Let's be clear; Kurtz is insane. He's a cult leader and war criminal who is only honest or 'rational' in so far as he has come up with his own twisted logic to justify his actions. In reality, this guy is fucking cuckoo and nothing he says carries any weight beyond the superficial.

A major theme of the film is how people cope with and justify the bad things they do. The journey through the river isn't one into morality or self-discovery but one into barbarism. The characters are thrust into a world where violence and exploitation are normalised and people like Kurtz have no way to continue other than wax philosophical.

There's no hidden truth Kurtz has uncovered about the nature of morality, just like there isn't any method he follows. Willard is only able to turn back down the river and return to civilisation as he sees through the BS that Kurtz (and the last guy the army sent) fell into.

I think both points can exist depending on if you chose to indulge him. But I feel this is definitely the most canonical take. Maybe the point is NOT to indulge him like you said and just recognize his lunacy for what it is.

Yes, but…Clean’s actions are not a premeditated choice. He was a child that was old enough to be given a gun and placed in a foreign land to kill. 
  
   Everything about stopping that boat was wrong and stupid. This was Chief following another bullshit Army directive that put the mission, his crew, and civilians in danger over a puppy.

So an interesting take that I think you can add to this is the notion of reason itself being polluted by the horror of existence. 

Its important to keep in mind yhat resistance to American and French colonialism in Vietnam can’t be disconnected from Buddhism. Even though a lot of the Marxist revolutionaries were not Buddhist, there is a Taoist tradition in vietnam that mixes with indigenous practices. 

So another comment here talks about how Kurtz isn’t rational, but actually he’s just diluted him himself into thinking that he is adhering to a code and that is why Willard is able to finally see through the manipulation and kill him in the end. 

I think the movie intentionally walks a razor’s edge between both sides: the Americans are just going through the old motions inherited from the botched french colony multiplied by their own distortions and biases (Karmas); and Kurz is essentially making a choice for action based on principals discerned from following the logic of the situation (Dharma). 

And then, yes, the reveal is that when Willard ultimately realizes that kurz is not enlightened, he carries out his own right action (dharma) of killing him to complete the mission for the equally amoral warmongers he’s dedicated his life to serving and cant now escape (karma). 

And so the wheel of suffering (the horror) is upheld. Which is specifically the whole point of the movie: outlining the toxicity and futility of power intervention/the illusion of control.

Thats how its an anti-war movie in a Buddhist context: The further outside you bring the war, the deeper inside yourself the war burrows itself.
His methods are unsound but they are effective.

Except Willard doesn't exactly "return to civilization" either. Here is what he says on his way to kill Kurtz:

>They were going to make me a major for this, and I wasn't even in their fking army anymore.

So clearly, he has much like Kurtz, disowned himself with the US military complex which is ostensibly the symbol of "civilization" in that environment. Nor does he see Kurtz's words as BS since he clearly seems to still hold admiration and sympathy for him in his monologues. If anything, Willard is now basically in the same state of mind as Kurtz was, except he somewhat decides that enough is enough anyway and leaves with Lance, much like how Kurtz wanted to be killed and for all this to be over with.
But Lance also joins Clean in gunning down the boat.

I would say Kurtz is the dark face of imperialism in general, not strictly limited to the US.

It's a retelling of Dante's Inferno, with the final scenes being the interaction with Lucifer/the colonel. I think Copolla is playing with this parallel and challenging our moral constructs in the end. Kurtz and his actions are both rational and horrifying. His morality is the only one that makes sense in the deeply immoral and thoroughly irrational context of imperialism and war. It's a sort of satanic morality. 

Great post OP.

I think he’s a lot like General Jack D. Ripper from Dr. Strangelove in the sense that he’s doing the job given to him too well. They’re both crazy, but it’s also true that the orders they were given were crazy and their actions were the natural conclusion of what their superiors were asking for.

Characterizing Kurtz (or anyone, really) as being “insane” or  “fucking cuckoo” isn’t terribly useful as it tends to serve no other purpose but flatten all nuance and shut down debate. There is no clinical definition of “cuckoo”, so what does it actually mean? 

You concede that Kurtz is capable of logic, albeit “twisted” to justify his actions. Don’t we all “twist” logic to justify, minimize and/or recontextualize our actions to varying degrees in order to make them palatable to others and to ourselves? Does this mean we’re all insane?
Just because something is immoral and abhorrent doesn’t mean it can’t also be rational.

Kurtz was an antihero and the irony and hypocrisy of his ordered assassination is his governments role in not only the war itself but the way it was waged. 

The contrast is between one beloved warlord (Kurtz) and the Warlord of all warlords (US Govt). Why do you think the previous assassin converted to his side? (Capt. Kolby).

No absolutely no and WTF. You might have had an argument for Kilgore but arguing that Kurtz is a good person makes it sound like you are intentionally giving the wrong answer for engagement or did not watch the movie.

I fully agree with the parallels you draw between Willard and Kurtz and you've put it well. To my mind. Kurtz appeals to a part of Willard as they have common experiences and are disillusioned with the army and war generally. But Willard ultaimately rejects Kurtz's philosophy when he kills him and leaves, which is why I said BS. Maybe calling it BS was crass of me but I think Willard is only empathising and recognising their common experiences rather than agreeing with any of Kurtz' conclusions.

By "return to civilisation" I only mean that Willard leaves Kurtz' compound/ cult rather than abandoning his mission; I'm not speculating on where he literally went. I'm not sure I'd agree that the US army represents civilisation in that environment. We see places that exist independently of the army. I haven't seen the film in a while but there's the plantation scene, Willard is staying in a city at the start of the film, and I think we see some villages. Kurtz can reject the army and Kurtz at the same time; that doesn't leave him with nowhere to go.
The film is based on heart of darkness after all

I didn't mean to be dismissive (and this was an interesting post btw, thank you!). I think there is some coherency to what Kurtz is saying, you're right, but I don't think that makes him rational or honest. I think Kurtz as a character gives the illusion of being rational with how he speaks and reasons but he is ultimately someone who has, in a very literal sense, gone insane.

I hear what you're saying and maybe the language I used was unhelpful. What I meant is that I see Kurtz as someone who is - very literally - insane. He can structure an argument - maybe even a compelling one to some people - but we need to remember the actions he is recontextualising, minimising and justifying are atrocities.
It’s a book that a lot of people had to read in high school and didn’t like so you could definitely find it at a used bookstore for very cheap. I personally love the book.

That's exactly what I thought. Kurtz is just a (more honest) reflection of the US military.

Yes. The toubling thing with Kurtz is that he is completely rational in his beliefs. Contrast him with a person like Kilgore, who does and orders horrifying things but dresses them up in a cloak of justifiability. "We're fighting to free them, so it's right to kill them," Kilgore might say. The difference with Kurtz is that he has completely dispensed with such BS. Killing is killing to him. There is no need to seek moral justification or excuses for your actions. This is why the generals want him dead. Not because of his actions, but because he has dropped the cloak that hides the grossness of such actions. Wilard understands this. He is kurtz in so many ways and this is excemplified in the boat scene where they gun down the family. They've just murdered this family yet still feel they need to treat the wounded. Wilard shoots the woman and it shocks everyone else because of how callous it looks. To Wilard though, it makes no difference. She was dead anyway so what's the point? This is Kurtz's philosophy. Dispense with all fake morality and just do what you're here to do. Kill.

Ultimately, Wilard chooses to reject Kurtz's philosophy, though it's debatable that he really does. He knows Kurtz is right, but also that he is insane and has to be put down. He may have only done it because, as he says, maybe Kurtz wanted him to do it and take the pain away.

As another metaphor, Kurtz is Satan sitting at the centre of hell.  The book Heart of Darkness, upon which Apocalypse Now was based, was representative of the nine rings of hell as in Dante’s Inferno with each progression further down the river getting crazier and crazier as he gets deeper into hell.  It is also about how people lose their humanity without the trappings of civilization to hold them back.

Yes, he was. Col. Kurtz is the only truly human being in the film, in the sense of being thoroughly conscious. The military apparatus is shown as dehumanizing, downplaying the weight of the massacre and violence. Kurtz is the only one who takes account of the meaning and weight of what is actually going on : war, genocide, dehumanization.

This, to me, is part of the sheer genius of this film. At the outset, we are the Hero embarking on a Journey to eliminate Evil. Along the way, the supposed heroism devolves into crass violence, absurdism, denial, madness. The silent protagonist (Willard) takes stock, observes. He notices things are more complex than they seemed.

At the end of the journey awaits not Evil, but Understanding. The journey itself was a journey into the "Heart of Darkness" (the book that inspired the film). Once he reaches the Heart of Darkness, Willard is able to Understand Kurtz, especially the fact that what seems like madness is the only sane response to a mad situation : war and genocide. Self-aware insanity is the only rational response, while the other characters range from denial, impulsiveness, narcotics, gamifying, distraction - anything to look the other way. Kurtz stares right into the abyss.

The end of the journey, the heart of the labyrinth, is the darkness at the heart of man. One man understands it and embodies it. He retains his humanity. The rest are like tools, being used for violence, splitting themselves away from what they are doing.

I entirely agree with your assessment of the film. Thank you for reminding me how great this masterpiece is.

Thanks for this analysis. I feel like I need to read Joseph Conrad’s Hearts of Darkness and rewatch the films before writing up a full review. 

I saw Eleanor Coppola’s documentary a number of years ago and I was thinking about it while reading your review. So it was good to see you mention it at the end (Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmakers Apocalypse from 1981).

Brando talked a lot with Francis about the role and chose his words carefully as Kurtz. And he was a bit of a crazy genius as well. I think a lot of different things added up to the choices made in the film. But certainly taking the words and actions at face value, your analysis makes sense. 

Wasn’t there an animal sacrifice? I wonder how that fits in. Also Kurtz created that society, or at least embedded himself in it so that also may have informed his new philosophy.

Eleanor Coppola caught word that a local tribe near the set of Kurtz's compound was going to sacrifice pigs and a water buffalo in a big ceremony. Initially Francis wasn't interested, but it was Eleanor who convinced him it to film it and as we know it ended up in the movie. I think there is a lot to be unpacked about the meaning of the sacrifice. The slaughter of the water buffalo parallels Kurtz's assassination in the sequential way it is presented and initially suggest that Kurtz's killing is not just an act of military duty but a ritualistic offering, symbolizing the end of his reign and his philosophical journey. A pessimistic view might be that neither sacrifices serve any grander purpose but to provide moralistic relief. If you believe in the tribalistic religion you would feel that the sacrifice of the buffalo has a higher purpose beyond providing meat, just as if you believe in the American Army you would believe Kurtz death signifies a turning point in the morality of the war. There's definitely more to be unpacked here.

I think that Chef also had a level of humanity, self awareness and consciousness about the situation too. He is the one who is most angry about the massacre on the Sampan, he talks about the pointlessness of the mission but continues on anyway, and he seems to know how his life will be wasted (almost accepting his fate). 


I also wonder if the three dead boat crew members represent the journey that Willard had already been on before the movie starts?  Clean’s death represents the death of youth, Chief’s death represents the loss of control, Chef’s death represents the loss of humanity.  Willard is in a fog of depression and substance abuse at the start of the film- perhaps only Lance surviving shows that to survive the madness of war requires almost a complete disconnection from reality (either through disassociation or just lots of drugs).

Interesting you mention *Dr. Strangelove* and General Jack D. Ripper.

I’ve always felt that *Apocalypse Now* was a very “Kubrick”-like film and that Coppola seemed to be using elements found in Kubrick’s war films for that film.

That’s not to say I feel Coppola somehow “ripped off” Kubrick: I consider *Apocalypse Now* (well, the theatrical cut anyway!) an absolutely brilliant movie.  But the influences I’ve always felt were there, apart from adapting Joseph Conrad’s novel.
